prompt: In New York, a blood alcohol content (BAC) of what level is evidence of intoxication (DWI)?
explanation: A BAC of .08 percent or higher is evidence of intoxication in New York. More than .05 is evidence of impairment (DWAI), and .18 or more is Aggravated DWI.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 55

prompt: Under New York law, a BAC of more than .05 percent (but below .08) is legal evidence of what?
choices: That your ability to drive is impaired (DWAI)
Nothing; it is below the legal limit
explanation: New York treats a BAC of more than .05 percent as legal evidence of impairment, which supports a Driving While Ability Impaired (DWAI) charge even though it is below .08.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 55

prompt: At what BAC does a New York driver face a charge of Aggravated DWI (Agg-DWI)?
explanation: A BAC of .18 percent or more is evidence of aggravated driving while intoxicated. A first Agg-DWI conviction brings at least a one-year revocation.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 55

prompt: Under New York's Zero Tolerance Law, what BAC range is a violation for a driver under 21?
explanation: The Zero Tolerance Law makes it a violation for a driver under 21 to have a measurable BAC of .02 to .07. A .02 BAC can come from just one drink.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 57

prompt: A 19-year-old is found at a DMV hearing to have driven with a .03 BAC. This is a first Zero Tolerance violation. What happens to the license?
choices: Nothing, because the BAC is under .05
It is suspended for six months
explanation: A first Zero Tolerance violation (BAC .02 to .07, under 21) brings a six-month suspension, plus a $100 suspension termination fee and a $125 civil penalty to get relicensed.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 57

prompt: A New York driver over age 21 refuses a chemical (breath) test for the first time after an arrest. What is the minimum license penalty?
choices: Revocation for at least six months
A fine only, with no license action
Revocation for at least one year
explanation: A first chemical test refusal by a driver over 21 brings a minimum one-year revocation, plus a $500 civil penalty before a new license can be issued.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, pp. 21, 23

prompt: You refuse a breath test after a DWI arrest, and later the court finds you not guilty of DWI. A DMV hearing confirms you refused the test. What happens?
choices: You must retake the written test but keep your license
Your license is still revoked for the refusal
Your license is returned because you were found not guilty
Only a warning is placed on your record
explanation: Refusal is a separate issue from guilt. If a DMV hearing confirms you refused, your license is revoked even if you are found not guilty of the alcohol or drug charge.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 56

prompt: What is the minimum license penalty for a first DWI conviction (.08 BAC or higher) for a New York driver 21 or older?
choices: Revocation for at least six months
Revocation for at least one year
explanation: A first DWI conviction carries a minimum six-month revocation. A first Aggravated DWI (.18+) carries at least a one-year revocation, and a first DWAI a 90-day suspension.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 20

prompt: What is the fine range for a first-offense DWI in New York (not counting surcharges)?
explanation: A first DWI (or DWAI-drug) is a misdemeanor with a fine of $500 to $1,000, up to one year in jail, and license revocation. $1,000 to $2,500 is the range for a first Aggravated DWI.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 58

prompt: What license penalty applies to a first conviction for Driving While Ability Impaired by alcohol (DWAI) in New York?
choices: No license penalty, only a fine
explanation: A first DWAI (alcohol) conviction is a traffic infraction with a $300 to $500 fine, up to 15 days in jail, and a 90-day license suspension.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 20

prompt: Under Leandra's Law, a driver who commits an alcohol-related driving offense with a child of what age in the vehicle can be charged with a felony?
explanation: Leandra's Law allows a class E felony charge, punishable by up to four years in prison, for alcohol-related driving offenses committed with a child under 16 in the vehicle.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 59

prompt: After a DWI conviction in New York, the court must order an ignition interlock on any vehicle the driver owns or operates for at least how long?
explanation: Courts must order anyone convicted of DWI or Aggravated DWI to install and maintain an ignition interlock for at least 12 months (the court may end it after six months if certain conditions are met).
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 59

prompt: Which statement about New York's open container law is correct?
choices: It applies only to the driver
Passengers may drink if the driver is sober
It applies only on highways, not city streets
It applies to both drivers and passengers on public roads
explanation: It is a traffic infraction for a driver or passenger in a motor vehicle on a public highway, street or road to drink alcohol or possess an open container of an alcoholic beverage. Passengers in vehicles like stretch limousines are exempt.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 57

prompt: What is the maximum fine for a first open container conviction in New York (not counting surcharges)?
explanation: A first open container conviction can bring a fine up to $150, plus a mandatory surcharge, a crime victim assistance fee, and possible imprisonment of 15 days.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 57

prompt: A passenger in a regular car on a New York street consumes cannabis while the car is moving. Under state law, this is:
choices: Only illegal if the driver also uses it
Legal because the passenger is not driving
Legal if the cannabis was bought legally
explanation: New York's open container law also makes it a traffic infraction for a driver or passenger in a motor vehicle on a public road to consume marijuana/cannabis.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 57

prompt: What is the minimum age to apply for a learner permit in New York?
explanation: You must be at least 16 to apply for a New York learner permit. Students who are 15 years and 11 months can take the written test online at participating high schools, but must be 16 to get the permit.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 11

prompt: How long must a New York junior learner permit be held before you can schedule a road test?
choices: At least six months, not counting any time it was suspended or revoked
explanation: A junior permit must be held for a minimum of six months, excluding any time it was suspended or revoked, before a road test can be scheduled.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 19

prompt: Before a junior driver's road test, the parent or guardian must certify how much supervised practice driving?
choices: At least 30 hours, including 5 at night
At least 60 hours, including 20 at night
At least 50 hours, including at least 15 hours after sunset
At least 40 hours, including 10 at night
explanation: Form MV-262 certifies at least 50 hours of supervised practice, with at least 15 hours after sunset. DMV also recommends at least 10 hours in moderate to heavy traffic.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 14

prompt: In New York, who may supervise a learner permit holder upstate (outside NYC and Long Island) during daytime hours?
choices: A licensed driver at least 21 years old with a license valid for the vehicle, seated in the front seat
Any licensed driver at least 18 years old
Any passenger who is 25 or older
explanation: A permit holder must be supervised by a licensed driver at least 21 years old, with a license valid for the vehicle being driven, who sits in the front seat.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 11

prompt: A 16-year-old with a junior learner permit wants to practice in New York City. Who may supervise?
choices: Only a parent, guardian, or driving instructor (age 21+ and properly licensed)
Any licensed driver age 21 or older
Any licensed driver age 18 or older
Any adult passenger, licensed or not
explanation: In Long Island and New York City, the supervising driver must be a parent, guardian or driving instructor (including a driver education teacher), age 21 or older with a valid license for the vehicle.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 13

prompt: With a junior learner permit, who may ride in the front passenger seat?
explanation: If you hold a junior permit, the only passenger allowed in the front seat is your supervising driver.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 13

prompt: What is the minimum age for a New York Class D (senior) driver license?
choices: 18, or 17 with a driver education Certificate of Completion
explanation: The Class D license minimum age is 18, or 17 with a driver education Student Certificate of Completion (MV-285) from an approved high school or college course.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 6

prompt: A 16-year-old has a New York junior license (Class DJ). How many passengers under age 21 may ride with them?
choices: Any number if a parent approves in writing
No more than one, unless they are immediate family members
explanation: A junior license holder cannot drive with more than one passenger under the age of 21 unless they are members of the driver's immediate family.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 15

prompt: Where may a New York junior license (Class DJ) holder NOT drive at all?
explanation: Under the regional restrictions, a junior licensee must not drive in New York City at any hour. Long Island and upstate have their own time and purpose limits.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 16

prompt: An upstate junior license holder wants to drive alone to a friend's house at 3 PM. Is this allowed?
choices: No, junior drivers must always have a parent in the car
Only if driving to school or work
Only with a written note from a parent
Yes, upstate junior drivers may drive unaccompanied from 5 AM to 9 PM
explanation: In upstate counties, a junior licensee may drive without being accompanied between 5 AM and 9 PM.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 16

prompt: An upstate junior license holder wants to drive at 11 PM. Which trip may they make alone?
choices: Anywhere, if no passengers are in the car
None; they may not drive at all after 9 PM
Directly between home and work or a school course
To a friend's house if they are back by midnight
explanation: Upstate, between 9 PM and 5 AM a junior licensee may drive alone only directly between home and employment or a school course. All other driving must be accompanied by a licensed parent, guardian or person in loco parentis.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 16

prompt: A junior driver is convicted of a serious traffic violation worth three or more points. What happens to the junior license?
choices: It is revoked for one year
explanation: A junior permit or license is suspended for 60 days for one serious violation (three points or more) or two other violations.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 19

prompt: A junior driver is convicted of texting while driving for the first time. What is the license penalty?
explanation: Junior permits and licenses, as well as probationary licenses, are suspended for 120 days on a first texting or cell phone conviction.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 19

prompt: If you are 18 or older when you pass your road test in New York, how long is your probation period?
explanation: Drivers who are 18 or older when they pass the road test, or who get a license after revocation, are on probation for six months.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 19

prompt: A new driver on probation is convicted of speeding. What happens?
choices: The license is revoked for one year
The probation is extended by one month
The license is suspended for 60 days, then a new six-month probation begins
Nothing extra, just the fine and points
explanation: A probationer convicted of speeding, DWAI, reckless driving, following too closely, a speed contest, or any two violations gets a 60-day suspension, followed by a new six-month probation.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 19

prompt: Before scheduling a New York road test, most new drivers must complete which course?
choices: An approved 5-hour Pre-Licensing Course (or high school/college driver education)
The Point and Insurance Reduction Program (defensive driving course)
explanation: You must complete an approved safe driving course: the 5-hour Pre-Licensing Course or a driver education course. The Point and Insurance Reduction Program (defensive driving) does NOT meet this requirement.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 14

prompt: What vision standard must you meet to pass the New York DMV vision test?
choices: 20/40 in at least one eye, with or without corrective lenses
explanation: To pass the vision test you must have 20/40 vision in at least one eye, with or without corrective lenses.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 10

prompt: To pass the New York written permit test, what must you score?
choices: At least 16 of 20 correct, with no road-sign errors
At least 14 of 20 correct, including all 4 road-sign questions
At least 14 of 20 correct, including at least 2 of the 4 road-sign questions
explanation: You must correctly answer at least 14 of the 20 questions, and you must get at least two of the four road-sign questions right.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 10

prompt: You move to a new address in New York. How soon must you notify the DMV?
explanation: If you change your address you must notify DMV within 10 days by mail (form MV-232) or online, and write the new address on the back of your license.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 17

prompt: You become a permanent New York resident and hold a valid license from another state. How soon must you get a New York license?
explanation: New residents must turn in their out-of-state license and get a New York license within 30 days of becoming a permanent resident.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 6

prompt: Which is New York's minimum liability insurance coverage for injury?
choices: $25,000 for one person and $50,000 for two or more people
$15,000 for one person and $30,000 for two or more people
$50,000 for one person and $100,000 for two or more people
$30,000 for one person and $60,000 for two or more people
explanation: New York requires $25,000/$50,000 for injury, $50,000/$100,000 for death, and $10,000 for property damage. The $50,000/$100,000 figures apply to death, not injury.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 27

prompt: What is New York's minimum property damage liability coverage?
explanation: Minimum liability coverage includes $10,000 against property damage in any one incident.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 27

prompt: Your auto insurance policy is about to end and you will not renew it. What should you do first?
choices: Mail the registration sticker to your insurance company
Notify the DMV within 90 days after it lapses
Turn in your license plates at a motor vehicle office before the insurance ends
Keep the plates and just stop driving the car
explanation: Before liability insurance expires, return the plates and get a receipt (FS-6T). Otherwise you may pay a civil penalty for each uninsured day or have your registration suspended; 90 uninsured days also suspends your license.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 27

prompt: What happens to your New York license if you are convicted of driving an uninsured vehicle?
choices: You receive points but keep your license
It is revoked for at least one year
It is suspended until you show proof of insurance
explanation: Driving, or letting someone drive, your uninsured vehicle, or a crash without insurance, results in at least a one-year revocation and a $750 civil penalty to relicense.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 21

prompt: Under the New York DMV point system, how many points within 24 months lead to a license suspension?
explanation: If you get 11 or more points within 24 months, DMV will suspend your license. Points count from the date of the violation.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 22

prompt: How many points can a DMV-approved Point and Insurance Reduction Program (crash prevention course) remove from your New York record?
explanation: A DMV-approved crash prevention course can reduce your point total by up to four points (and may lower insurance premiums). It cannot prevent a mandatory suspension or revocation.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 22

prompt: A New York driver gets six points within 18 months. Besides the fines, what must they pay?
choices: Nothing extra unless they reach 11 points
A $25 fee to reinstate their points
A Driver Responsibility Assessment of $100 per year for three years
explanation: Six points in any 18-month period triggers a Driver Responsibility Assessment of $100 per year for three years, plus $25 per year for each additional point.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 23

prompt: New York is a "primary enforcement" seat belt state. What does this mean?
choices: Seat belts are required only on highways
An officer can stop you just because someone in the vehicle is not wearing a seat belt
You can be ticketed for a seat belt only after being stopped for something else
Only the driver must wear a seat belt
explanation: In a primary enforcement state, a police officer can pull you over solely because you or a passenger is not wearing a seat belt. The law also applies to visitors.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 48

prompt: In New York, which passengers are personally responsible for wearing their own seat belt and can be fined up to $50?
explanation: Passengers 16 or older must be belted, one person per belt, and can be fined up to $50. The driver is responsible for passengers under 16.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 48

prompt: You are driving with a 12-year-old passenger who is not buckled up. What penalty can you, the driver, receive?
choices: No penalty; the child is fined
A warning for a first offense
A fine of $25 to $100 and three points for each violation
explanation: The driver must make sure every passenger under 16 is properly restrained, and can be fined $25 to $100 and receive three points for each violation.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 48

prompt: Under New York law, a child under what age must ride in a federally approved child safety seat?
explanation: A child under age four must be restrained in a federally approved child safety seat attached by a seat belt or LATCH system.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 48

prompt: What does New York law require for a 5-year-old passenger of average size?
choices: No restraint if riding in the back seat
An appropriate child restraint such as a booster seat used with a lap and shoulder belt
explanation: Children ages 4 through 7 must use an appropriate federally approved child restraint system, commonly a booster seat with a lap and shoulder belt. A seat belt alone is not an appropriate child restraint for them.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 48

prompt: Under New York law, a child must ride rear-facing until at least what age (unless they outgrow the seat's rear-facing limits)?
explanation: A child must be restrained rear-facing until age two or until reaching the highest rear-facing weight or height limit allowed by the car seat manufacturer.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 48

prompt: Which use of a mobile phone is legal for a fully licensed adult driver in New York?
choices: Holding the phone to your ear at a red light
Reading a text while stopped in traffic
Holding the phone to listen on speaker
explanation: It is a traffic infraction to speak into or listen to a hand-held phone while driving, but a hands-free phone (no hands needed to communicate) may be used at any time.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 52

prompt: How many points does a first conviction for using a hand-held cell phone while driving add to a New York driving record?
explanation: Hand-held phone use carries a fine up to $200 for a first offense and five license points. Hands-free phones may be used at any time.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 52

prompt: What is the maximum fine for a third texting-while-driving offense committed within 18 months in New York?
explanation: Texting fines are up to $200 for a first offense, up to $250 for a second within 18 months, and up to $450 for a third or subsequent offense within 18 months.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 52

prompt: When no speed limit is posted, what is New York State's general maximum speed limit?
explanation: If no limit is posted, drive no more than 55 mph. Some cities have lower limits that are not always posted.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 47

prompt: What is the speed limit in New York City when no other limit is posted?
explanation: The speed limit is 25 mph in New York City unless another limit is posted.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 47

prompt: What is the highest speed limit New York expressways can be posted at, according to the Driver's Manual?
explanation: The expressway speed limit is normally 55 mph but can be posted at 65 mph in some rural areas.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 62

prompt: You are driving 50 mph on a foggy, slippery expressway posted at 55 mph. Can you be ticketed for speeding?
choices: Only if you cause a crash
Yes, for driving at a speed not reasonable for conditions
No, because you are under the posted limit
No, because the minimum speed is 45 mph
explanation: Posted limits are maximums. On a hazardous highway, even 50 mph can be ticketed as a speed "not reasonable" for the conditions.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 47

prompt: The New York Driver's Manual recommends a following distance of at least how many seconds in good conditions?
explanation: Use the two-second rule: when the vehicle ahead passes a fixed object, you should not reach it before counting "one thousand one, one thousand two."
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 47

prompt: In bad weather or when following a large truck, New York's manual says to increase your following count to at least:
explanation: In bad weather and when following large trucks, increase the two-second count to at least three or four seconds.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 47

prompt: You are caught speeding in a New York highway work zone on a weekend when no workers are present. What happens to the fine?
choices: It is doubled only if workers are present
It is waived for a first offense
It is doubled, even when workers are not present
It is the normal fine because no workers are there
explanation: Speeding fines double in work zones, even when the workers or work vehicles are not there.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 49

prompt: You are on a two-way road and an ambulance with lights and siren approaches from the opposite direction. What must you do in New York?
choices: Stop where you are, even in the travel lane
Pull over to the right edge of the road and stop until it passes
Keep driving, since it is in the other lane
explanation: You must pull over and stop for an emergency vehicle even if it is headed toward you in the opposite lane of a two-way roadway.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 35

prompt: You are in the middle of an intersection when a fire truck with flashing red lights approaches. What should you do?
choices: Drive out of the intersection, then pull over to the right and stop
Back up out of the intersection
Turn left to get out of its way
explanation: If you are in an intersection, drive out of it before you pull over. Then stop at the right edge until the emergency vehicle passes.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 35

prompt: In New York, a personal car showing a flashing blue light is most likely driven by:
choices: A volunteer firefighter responding to an alarm
explanation: Volunteer firefighters may display blue lights on personal vehicles, and volunteer ambulance or rescue squad members may display green lights. These are not authorized emergency vehicles.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 35

prompt: A personal car with a flashing green light comes up behind you. What does New York law require?
choices: You must speed up to clear the lane
You are not required to yield, but should yield as a courtesy if safe
You must pull over and stop as for an ambulance
explanation: Green lights mark volunteer ambulance or rescue members' personal vehicles. They are not authorized emergency vehicles and must obey traffic laws; you are not required to yield, but should as a courtesy if safe.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 35

prompt: Under New York's Move Over Law, what must you do on a multi-lane interstate when passing a police car stopped on the shoulder with its lights flashing?
choices: Move over only if an officer is outside the car
Slow down and move out of the lane next to it, if you can do so safely
Only slow down to 10 mph below the limit
explanation: Drivers must reduce speed on all roads, and on parkways, interstates and other multi-lane controlled-access roads must also move out of the adjacent lane unless traffic or hazards prevent it.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 35

prompt: Does New York's Move Over Law apply to a tow truck stopped on the shoulder with amber flashing lights?
choices: Yes, it covers hazard vehicles with amber lights
No, it covers only police cars
No, it covers only fire trucks and ambulances
explanation: The Move Over Law covers authorized emergency vehicles and hazard vehicles (like tow trucks and snow plows) displaying amber hazard lights, including amber-and-blue combinations.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 35

prompt: On a New York parkway, a regular passenger car with a flat tire is stopped on the shoulder. Does the Move Over Law apply?
choices: No, it applies only to vehicles with emergency lights
No, it applies only to police vehicles
Only if the driver waves you over
Yes, drivers must also move over for vehicles stopped on the shoulder of a parkway or controlled-access highway
explanation: New York's Move Over Law also requires drivers to move over for motor vehicles parked, stopped or standing on the shoulder or any part of a parkway or controlled-access highway.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 35

prompt: A school bus is stopped with red lights flashing on the opposite side of a divided highway. What must you do in New York?
choices: Stop only if children are crossing
Stop; New York requires stopping even on the opposite side of a divided highway
Continue carefully, because a median separates you
explanation: New York's school bus law applies on all roadways. You must stop for a school bus with flashing red lights even if it is on the opposite side of a divided highway.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 40

prompt: When you stop behind a school bus with flashing red lights in New York, how far away should you stop?
explanation: Traffic from either direction must stop before reaching the bus, and you should stop at least 20 feet away.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 40

prompt: What happens to your New York license if you are convicted of passing a stopped school bus three times within three years?
choices: It is revoked for at least six months
It is revoked for five years
explanation: Fines range from at least $250 for a first violation up to $1,000 for three violations in three years, and three convictions in three years bring a revocation of at least six months.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 40

prompt: A blind pedestrian with a white cane starts across at an unmarked crosswalk, but your light is green. What must you do?
choices: Proceed, because you have the green light
Sound your horn to warn them
explanation: New York's special right-of-way law requires you to always yield to blind pedestrians using a guide dog or a white or metal cane at a marked or unmarked crosswalk, even if signals are not in their favor.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 67

prompt: You are driving in Manhattan and stopped at a red light. There is no sign about turns. May you turn right on red?
choices: Yes, if no pedestrians are present
No, turning on red is not allowed in New York City unless a sign permits it
explanation: Outside New York City, right turns on red are allowed after a full stop unless prohibited. In New York City, you may not turn on red unless a sign permits it.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 31

prompt: Outside New York City, when may you make a LEFT turn on a steady red light?
choices: When turning from a one-way road onto another one-way road, after a full stop and yielding
explanation: A left turn on red is allowed only from a one-way road into another one-way road, after a full stop and yielding to traffic and pedestrians.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 31

prompt: New York law requires you to signal a turn or lane change at least how far ahead?
explanation: You must signal a turn or lane change with turn lights or hand signals at least 100 feet ahead.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 36

prompt: Under New York law, you may not make a U-turn where other drivers cannot see your vehicle from how far away in either direction?
explanation: You cannot make a U-turn near the top of a hill, a curve or any location where other drivers cannot see your vehicle from 500 feet away in either direction.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 37

prompt: Where are U-turns illegal in New York even if no sign prohibits them?
choices: At any intersection with a traffic light
In New York City business districts and in school zones
explanation: U-turns are illegal in NYC business districts, in school zones, where NO U-TURN signs are posted, near hills or curves without 500 feet of visibility, and on limited-access expressways.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 37

prompt: On a two-way road, you may not pass on the left within how many feet of a railroad crossing?
explanation: You cannot pass on the left within 100 feet of a railroad crossing on a two-way roadway, or within 100 feet of a bridge, tunnel or viaduct when your view is obstructed.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 39

prompt: When passing on the left on a two-way road, you must be able to return to the right lane before an oncoming vehicle comes within how many feet?
explanation: You cannot pass if you cannot safely return to the right lane before any oncoming vehicle comes within 200 feet of you.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 39

prompt: How does New York law require you to pass a bicyclist you are overtaking from behind?
choices: On the right, as close to the curb as possible
Only after honking to warn the cyclist
Within the same lane if the cyclist moves to the edge
On the left, at a safe distance, until you are clear of the bicycle
explanation: When overtaking a bicyclist, the law requires you to pass on the left at a safe distance until the bicycle has been cleared. Reduce speed, since air pressure can push the rider off balance.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 39

prompt: How close to a fire hydrant may you park in New York?
choices: No closer than 15 feet, unless a licensed driver stays in the vehicle
explanation: You cannot park, stop or stand within 15 feet of a fire hydrant, unless a licensed driver remains in the vehicle to move it in an emergency.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 43

prompt: In New York, parking or standing is not allowed within how many feet of a crosswalk at an intersection?
explanation: Parking or standing is not allowed within 20 feet of a crosswalk at an intersection.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 43

prompt: How far must you park from a traffic light, STOP sign, or YIELD sign in New York?
explanation: Parking or standing is not allowed within 30 feet of a traffic light, STOP sign or YIELD sign.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 43

prompt: In New York, you may not park within how many feet of a railroad crossing?
explanation: You cannot park your vehicle within 50 feet of a railroad crossing (and you may never park, stop or stand on the tracks).
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 43

prompt: You want to park across the street from a fire station driveway. How far from the driveway must you be?
explanation: Parking or standing is not allowed within 20 feet of a fire station driveway on the same side, or within 75 feet on the opposite side of the road.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 43

prompt: After parallel parking in New York, your wheels may be no more than how far from the curb?
explanation: In your final parallel-parked position, your wheels must be no more than one foot (30 cm) from the curb.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 42

prompt: In New York, what may you do where a NO STANDING sign is posted?
choices: Stop only briefly to pick up or drop off passengers, without leaving the vehicle
Stop to load or unload merchandise
Stop only to obey traffic signals; no passenger stops at all
explanation: A NO STANDING sign allows only a temporary stop to load or discharge passengers, and the driver cannot exit the vehicle. Loading merchandise is allowed under a NO PARKING sign, not NO STANDING.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 43

prompt: When does New York law require you to use your headlights?
choices: From one hour after sunset to one hour before sunrise
Only when visibility is under 500 feet
From 1/2 hour after sunset to 1/2 hour before sunrise, when visibility is under 1,000 feet, and when using wipers
explanation: Headlights are required from one-half hour after sunset to one-half hour before sunrise, when visibility is less than 1,000 feet, and whenever you use your wipers for rain, snow, sleet or fog.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 63

prompt: It is a cloudy afternoon and you turn on your wipers to clear light rain. What does New York law require?
choices: Turn on your headlights (daytime running lights do not count)
explanation: New York requires headlights whenever conditions require windshield wipers to clear rain, snow, sleet or fog. Daytime running lights and parking lights do not qualify.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 63

prompt: In New York, you must switch to low beams when an oncoming vehicle is within how many feet?
explanation: Your headlights must be on low beam within 500 feet of an oncoming vehicle and within 200 feet of a vehicle ahead of you.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 63

prompt: In New York, you must dim your high beams when you are following another vehicle within how many feet, even if it is in a different lane?
explanation: Use low beams within 200 feet of a vehicle ahead of you, even if it is in a different lane, and within 500 feet of an oncoming vehicle.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 63

prompt: During what period may tires with metal studs be used in New York State?
explanation: Tires with metal studs can be used in New York State only from October 16 through April 30.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 64

prompt: When railroad crossing lights are flashing or the gates are coming down, how far from the tracks must you stop in New York?
explanation: Flashing red lights, lowered gates or a bell mean you must stop at least 15 feet from the tracks and wait until the lights and bell stop and the gates are fully up.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 61

prompt: Under New York law, what must you NOT do when approaching or passing a horse on the road?
explanation: It is illegal to sound your horn when you approach or pass a horse. You must drive at a reasonable speed and keep a safe distance.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 76

prompt: Where must Class B and Class C mopeds be driven in New York?
choices: In the right lane, as far to the right as possible
In any lane, like a car
explanation: Class B and C mopeds may be driven only in the right lane as far right as possible (except when turning left). Mopeds are not allowed on expressways unless signs permit.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 74

prompt: A motorcycle is riding near the left side of your lane. In New York, may you move into the same lane space to pass it?
choices: Yes, if the lane is wide enough
Yes, if the rider waves you by
No; a motorcycle is entitled to the full width of the lane
explanation: Give a motorcycle the same full-lane width as other vehicles. Never move into the same lane space as a motorcycle, even if the lane is wide and the motorcycle is to one side.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 39

prompt: In New York, you must file a crash report with the DMV if property damage to any one person is at least how much?
explanation: You must report any crash involving death or personal injury, or $1,000 or more in damage to the property of any one person, using form MV-104.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 77

prompt: How long do you have to file a required crash report (MV-104) with the New York DMV?
explanation: You must file a report with DMV within 10 days of the crash. Reporting to your insurance company does not satisfy this obligation.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 77

prompt: You reported a crash with $2,000 in damage to your insurance company. Do you still need to report it to the New York DMV?
choices: Yes, within 10 days; reporting to your insurer does not satisfy the law
No, the insurer reports it for you
Only if the police were called
explanation: Reporting to your insurer does not end your legal obligation. You must file with DMV within 10 days for damage of $1,000 or more to one person's property; failure to report is a misdemeanor.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 77

prompt: In New York, leaving the scene of a crash that caused personal injury is:
choices: A traffic infraction with a small fine
Legal if you leave a note
Legal if no police are present
explanation: Leaving the scene of a property-damage crash is a traffic violation, but leaving the scene of a crash involving injury or death is a criminal violation.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 77

prompt: How far before an expressway exit ramp should you signal in New York?
choices: Signaling is not required to exit
explanation: Get into the correct lane ahead of time and signal your exit at least 100 feet before you reach the exit ramp.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 62

prompt: Under New York law, where may you NEVER make a U-turn, even if a path connects both sides?
choices: At an intersection with a green arrow
explanation: You can never make a U-turn on a limited-access expressway, even if paths connect your side with the other side.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 37

prompt: Under New York law, what protective gear must every motorcyclist wear?
choices: Eye protection only if there is no windshield
No gear is required for adults
An approved helmet and approved eye protection (goggles or a face shield)
explanation: New York requires motorcyclists to wear approved helmets and goggles or a face shield. The helmet requirement is not limited by age.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 71

prompt: Your motorcycle has a windshield. Do you still need approved eye protection in New York?
choices: Yes, eye protection is required even with a windshield
No, the windshield replaces eye protection
explanation: Motorcyclists must wear approved eye protection even if the motorcycle is equipped with a windshield.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 73

prompt: In New York, may a motorcyclist ride between lanes of cars or share a lane with a car?
choices: Yes, if the car moves to one side
No; a motorcyclist cannot pass or share a lane with a vehicle that is not a motorcycle
Yes, in slow traffic under 30 mph
explanation: A motorcyclist cannot pass or share a lane with another motor vehicle that is not a motorcycle, so lane splitting is not allowed.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 71

prompt: In New York, what is the largest number of motorcycles that may ride side by side in a single lane?
explanation: Two motorcyclists are allowed to ride side-by-side in a single lane; state law (VTL 1252) forbids riding more than two abreast in one lane.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 71; NY Vehicle and Traffic Law § 1252(d)

prompt: With a New York motorcycle learner permit or junior motorcycle license, who may ride as your passenger?
choices: No one except your supervising driver
explanation: A learner permit or junior license for a motorcycle or moped does not allow you to carry any passenger except your supervising driver.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 17

prompt: When a New York motorcycle permit holder practices, how close must the supervising driver stay?
choices: In sight of the rider at all times, by law
explanation: The supervising driver must be licensed for the same class of motorcycle and exercise supervision by remaining within one-quarter mile; DMV strongly recommends the supervisor be able to see you at all times.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 17

prompt: What is the minimum age for a New York Class M (unrestricted) motorcycle license?
choices: 18, or 17 with a driver education Certificate of Completion
explanation: Class M requires age 18, or 17 with a driver education Certificate of Completion. The Junior Motorcycle license (Class MJ) is available at 16 with junior restrictions.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 7

prompt: In New York, when must a motorcycle's headlight and taillight be on?
choices: Whenever the motorcycle is being ridden
Only when visibility is under 1,000 feet
explanation: Headlights and taillights on motorcycles must be illuminated when driving, day or night.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 71

prompt: Your New York motorcycle insurance expires for the winter. Must you turn in the motorcycle's plate?
choices: Only if the motorcycle is stored outdoors
No; motorcycles must be insured, but the plate need not be turned in when coverage ends
explanation: Motorcycles must be insured, but unlike cars, you are not required to turn in the plate when motorcycle insurance is discontinued or expires.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 27

prompt: For a New York motorcycle road test, what must the applicant bring in addition to the motorcycle?
choices: A passenger to ride on the motorcycle
A car or truck and a licensed driver to transport the license examiner
A second motorcycle for the examiner
explanation: Motorcycle applicants must bring a car or truck and a licensed driver to transport the license examiner during the road test.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 14

prompt: A New York teen gets a junior learner permit on their 16th birthday. What is the earliest age they could get a junior license (Class DJ)?
choices: 16 and a half, after holding the permit for six months
16, on the same day as the permit
17, after holding the permit for one year
explanation: The Class DJ junior license has a minimum age of 16, but a junior permit must be held at least six months before a road test can be scheduled, so the earliest is 16 and a half.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, pp. 6, 19

prompt: Some New York highways post a minimum speed limit. Why does driving below it matter?
choices: It interferes with traffic flow and creates a dangerous condition
It only matters for trucks and buses
It is allowed whenever the right lane is open
explanation: Some highways have minimum speed limits to keep traffic flowing smoothly. Driving slower than the minimum can interfere with traffic flow and create a dangerous condition.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 47

prompt: Under New York's statewide rules, when may you park, stop or stand inside an intersection?
choices: Only when signs or parking meters permit it
Whenever your hazard lights are on
For up to five minutes to unload passengers
explanation: You cannot park, stop or stand in an intersection unless signs or parking meters permit it. Hazard lights or a quick passenger stop do not make it legal.
ref: New York State Driver's Manual, p. 43
